The best chain on garnet is QB7-QB12-QB11, with QB12 in the middle. I read garnet's current default calibration (set f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade). It lists 28 CZ pairs, and every pair has an IRB CZ fidelity. I checked every chain of 3 connected qubits. The CZ fidelity of QB7-QB12 is 0.99802. The CZ fidelity of QB12-QB11 is 0.99869. Their product is 0.99671, which is the highest of all chains. The next best chain is QB12-QB11-QB16, with a product of 0.99469.

I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly those physical qubits. It puts QB12 into an equal mix of 0 and 1. Then it copies that state onto QB7 and onto QB11. Each copy uses one CZ gate with single-qubit rotations around it. The circuit uses only two CZ gates, on QB12-QB7 and QB12-QB11. It measures all 3 qubits. A noiseless simulation of this exact circuit gives 000 half the time and 111 half the time. I ran it once on garnet:mock with 200 shots (job 01a160a5-a220-7524-a35d-f7ad7390fc13). The server's copy of the job shows 2 CZ gates and measurements on QB7, QB12, QB11, with 200 shots. It cost 0 credits.

The counts are 000: 55, 001: 41, 110: 53, 111: 51. Bits are in the order QB7, QB12, QB11. The mock does not simulate the circuit. It returns random-looking results, so the 001 and 110 outcomes do not show an error in the circuit. On a real QPU, a good GHZ run would give mostly 000 and 111. That result would show entanglement. The three qubits would have no set value on their own, but they would always agree with each other.

The chain choice shows a practical rule. Each CZ gate adds its own small error, and the errors combine. Multiplying the two fidelities gives a rough estimate of how well the two entangling gates work together. That is why the chain with the highest product is the best place to run the circuit.
